column1: # The alphabet, and the thing it is actually for.

column2: spanish
column3: english

column1: # Leave the id off a new row — omit the column entirely, do not leave it empty.
# An alphabet is taught as a recital and used as an exchange. Nobody needs to
# chant twenty-seven names; they need to give a surname over the phone, read a
# booking code back, and ask whether a word has a `be` or a `uve` in it. So the
# recital is two sentences here and the rest is the exchange.
# Nine letters have no word card, and it is not an omission. `a`, `e`, `i`, `o`
# and `u` are named after themselves, and `de`, `te`, `ve` and `ese` are spelled
# exactly like a preposition, a pronoun, an imperative and a demonstrative —
# each already the most common word of its kind in the pack. A second lexeme for
# any of them would make the ordinary word ambiguous in every sentence it
# appears in, which is a high price for a card saying that `te` is also a
# letter. They are taught below in running text, where the context settles it.

column2: El alfabeto español tiene veintisiete letras.
column3: The Spanish alphabet has twenty-seven letters.
column6: Twenty-nine until 2010, when ch and ll stopped counting as letters of their own. An older textbook will say twenty-nine.

column2: Las cinco vocales se llaman como suenan.
column3: The five vowels are called the way they sound.
column6: So the names of a, e, i, o and u need no learning — which is why the letters worth drilling are the consonants.

column2: La eñe es la letra del español.
column3: The eñe is the Spanish letter.

column2: La eñe está en año, en mañana y en niño.
column3: The eñe is in año, in mañana and in niño.

column2: La hache no suena nunca.
column3: The letter H is never pronounced.
column6: Which is why hola and ola sound identical, and why a Spanish speaker writing English drops the h.

column2: Hache es la única letra muda.
column3: H is the only silent letter.

column2: ¿Se escribe con be o con uve?
column3: Is it written with a B or a V?
column6: The most useful question in this file: be and uve sound the same in Spanish, so this is asked constantly by native speakers too.

column2: Vaca con uve, baca con be.
column3: Vaca with a V, baca with a B.

column2: Se escribe con be, como en bueno.
column3: It is written with a B, as in bueno.

column2: La ge y la jota suenan igual delante de e.
column3: G and J sound the same before an e.

column2: Gente se escribe con ge.
column3: Gente is written with a G.

column2: México se escribe con equis.
column3: México is written with an X.

column2: La cu siempre va con u.
column3: Q always goes with a U.

column2: La zeta y la ce suenan igual delante de e.
column3: Z and C sound the same before an e.

column2: La ye antes se llamaba i griega.
column3: The letter Y used to be called i griega.
column6: Renamed ye in 2010. Most speakers over thirty still say i griega, so both are worth knowing.

column2: En México dicen ve corta, no uve.
column3: In Mexico they say ve corta, not uve.

column2: Mi apellido lleva dos eles.
column3: My surname has two Ls.

column2: Perro lleva dos erres.
column3: Perro has two Rs.

column2: ¿Cómo se escribe tu nombre?
column3: How do you write your name?

column2: ¿Me lo deletreas, por favor?
column3: Could you spell it for me, please?

column2: Te lo deletreo despacio.
column3: I will spell it for you slowly.

column2: Repite la última letra, por favor.
column3: Say the last letter again, please.

column2: Es una eme, no una ene.
column3: It is an M, not an N.

column2: ¿Con hache o sin hache?
column3: With an H or without?

column2: La primera letra es una jota.
column3: The first letter is a J.

column2: Hay una ka en kilo.
column3: There is a K in kilo.

column2: La efe de foto.
column3: F for foto.

column2: La pe de padre y la be de bueno.
column3: P for padre and B for bueno.

column2: Buenos días, quiero hacer una reserva.
column3: Good morning, I would like to make a booking.

column2: Muy bien. ¿Su nombre, por favor?
column3: Very good. Your name, please?

column2: Elena Gómez.
column3: Elena Gómez.

column2: ¿Me lo deletrea, por favor?
column3: Could you spell it for me, please?

column2: Ge, o con acento, eme, e, zeta.
column3: G, O with an accent, M, E, Z.
column6: The accent is spoken, not skipped: Gomez without it is a different surname.

column2: ¿Con ge de gente?
column3: With a G as in gente?

column2: Sí, con ge. Y Elena con una ele.
column3: Yes, with a G. And Elena with one L.

column2: Perfecto. ¿Para qué día?
column3: Perfect. For what day?

column2: Para el viernes.
column3: For Friday.
